sm: Grammar Girl Mignon Fogarty welcomes Jeremy Butterfield, former editor in chief at Collins Dictionaries, editor of the 2015 Fowler's Dictionary of Modern English Usage, and author of The Metaphor Zoo. He says the book began during lockdown, when a small book on metaphor made him notice how often people are turned into animals, and his research snowballed from a chapter on birds. English loves animals, he says, because they are the group next to us in the traditional Great Chain of Being and give a huge range of expression, from sharks to puppy eyes, top dogs and underdogs. Some metaphors are centuries old, while herding cats is first recorded in the Oxford English Dictionary in 1986. He thinks most people no longer picture the animals, and that language is a reef of dead metaphors.

Butterfield explains conceptual metaphor theory, where a mental metaphor such as life is a journey produces linguistic expressions like the first step in a career. His book's underlying idea is that human is animal, with sub-metaphors such as human sound is animal sound, and human families are bird families, as in empty nest, cuckoo in the nest and rule the roost. He also covers embodied and orientational metaphors, like happiness is up and anger is heat, and the newer reach out. The bee's knees was one of many 1920s coinings, including the snake's toenails and the sardine's whiskers, of which only the bee's knees and cat's whiskers survive. On dogs, he says the origin of the word dog is unknown, as with pig, hog, frog and stag, and that the Old English word was hound.

Mignon asks about man's best friend, which Butterfield says dates only to 1841, from a British military magazine, possibly linked to improved status for dogs in Victorian society. Dog metaphors range from yanking someone's chain and rattling their cage to letting someone off the leash and rabid dog, and the Oxford English Dictionary lists 270 meanings of dog, perhaps twenty of them metaphors or idioms. Asked why American metaphors are so vivid, he guesses Americans take a less restrained, more frontier approach to language. He adds that some words thought of as American, such as honey as a term of address, are actually old British ones. He then mentions that the pug was a royal dog brought over in the late seventeenth century, and that it is popular again.

Butterfield describes an eighteenth century society, the Order of the Pug, set up by German Catholics who could not become Freemasons. Members scratched at the door, were barked at, and kissed a porcelain pug's bottom, and the club lasted about ten years. He explains hush puppies through dogs and puppies meaning feet, and the story of fried corn fritters thrown to dogs. Birds supply the most body part metaphors, such as eagle eyed and swan necked, probably because we see them every day, and also take somebody under your wing. For cats, he cites a cat in gloves catches no mice, meaning don't pussyfoot, and says wildcat started with unreliable Midwest banks before becoming strikes in the 1930s. They also discuss eggcorns such as give up the goat and barefaced spelled with bear.

Butterfield discusses more eggcorns, including coming home to roast for roost, damp squid for damp squib, and bare-knuckle fight spelled with bear. He says he now sees metaphors everywhere and circles them in whatever he reads. Mignon notes that AI writing often produces odd, off metaphors, and he says that would not surprise him, since translation programs struggle with idioms. He says the book is The Metaphor Zoo, and that he can be found at his website, on Bluesky and on X. Mignon adds that a bonus segment will cover Fowler's Modern English Usage, which Butterfield edited.
